question: According to the definition of limit, explain why the sequence \(a_j = |x-x_0|^j\) raised to the power \(1/j\) has a limit and what that limit is, and how this fact is used in the proof to relate the convergence of the series to the inequality \(|x-x_0|<\rho\).
answer: The sequence simplifies to \(|x-x_0|\) for every \(j\), so its limit is \(|x-x_0|\). By the definition of limit, for any \(\epsilon>0\) we can choose \(N=1\) such that \(|a_j - |x-x_0||<\epsilon\) for all \(j\ge N\). This limit is the value \(r\) in the root test, and the proof uses the condition \(|x-x_0|<\rho\) where \(\rho=1/r\) to determine convergence.

question: Using the root test definition, explain why when the limit \(r\) equals zero (hence \(\rho=\infty\)), the series converges absolutely for every real \(x\), and how the absolute value \(|x-x_0|\) appears in this conclusion.
answer: If \(r=0\), then \(\rho=1/r=\infty\). The root test states the series converges absolutely whenever \(|x-x_0|<\rho\). Since \(\rho\) is infinite, the inequality \(|x-x_0|<\infty\) holds for all real \(x\). Thus the series converges absolutely for every \(x\). The absolute value appears as the distance from \(x\) to the center \(x_0\), which is always finite.
